general.temas: Recurring stories include the conviction for starting the Palisades fire, artificial intelligence and its effects on markets and education, and concerns about changes to a federal health committee. There are also reports on crime and safety, as well as political decisions and disputes. Only the New York Post highlights the bedbug infestation at New York City's 911 call center.
general.motivo_crispacion: The level of tension is moderate: changes to the federal health committee have raised concerns about possible political interference, while a court has questioned the passage of a Biden-era law. In Los Angeles, the controller accuses the city council of trying to weaken the mayor. News about immigration and violence also generates tension. By contrast, cooperation on border security between Trump and Texas's Democratic governor-elect, along with education, sports and entertainment coverage, balances the overall picture.

The New York Times.resumen:
- Artificial intelligence features prominently in stories about cybersecurity risks and tensions between Wall Street and Silicon Valley.
- Two articles examine immigration training problems and changes that could make it harder to fund transportation under Trump.
- A health committee holds a tumultuous first meeting with RFK Jr.'s appointees after months of paralysis.
- The Mexican military captures El Chapo Isidro in a violent operation; another piece recounts his career.
- The front page includes an interview with Hakeem Jeffries, political opinion and stories about culture, family caregiving and Thanksgiving.
The New York Times.motivo_populismo: The tone is predominantly factual, although expressions such as “cascade of problems” and “autocrats, tech lords” add drama and disparagement, the latter in an opinion piece.
The New York Times.sesgo: The selection highlights problems associated with Trump policies and includes an interview with a Democratic leader and a column critical of the administration. It also emphasizes the risks and economic tensions linked to artificial intelligence.

The Washington Post.resumen:
- Trump's press conference with Vance and Rubio raises questions about the 2028 presidential election; Trump and the Texas governor-elect agree to cooperate on border security.
- A court questions the passage of a pandemic-era law through proxy voting; members of a federal health panel warn of possible political interference.
- A man is convicted of starting the Palisades fire and a gang is charged with stealing more than $22 million in goods from trains.
- U.S. stocks enter correction territory amid concerns about technology and artificial intelligence; pilot programs test drones for transporting medical supplies.
- The front page includes human-interest stories about a recovered ring and an adopted dog, a profile of baseball player Bob Boone and news about Fiona the hippo.
The Washington Post.motivo_populismo: The tone is predominantly factual, although expressions such as “may have saved her life” and references to the deadly fire add emotional weight; there is no evident opposition between the people and the elites.
The Washington Post.sesgo: The selection pays attention to decisions and potential conflicts involving the Trump administration, but also covers its agreement with a Democratic governor. These headlines do not reveal a conclusive partisan bias.

The Wall Street Journal.resumen:
- New York's billionaire police chief and its socialist mayor have formed an unlikely alliance.
- A California jury convicted a man of starting the deadly 2025 Palisades fire.
- Several officers were accused of misconduct in connection with a fatal shooting in South Carolina.
- Education features in several stories: cellphone restrictions, shorter degree programs, racial discrimination, grade disputes and a $3 billion donation.
- The front page also covers changes at major law firms, life on an aircraft carrier and the death of Fiona the hippo.
The Wall Street Journal.motivo_populismo: The language is predominantly factual, although expressions such as a pilot's “worst fear” and the contrast between “billionaire” and “socialist” add drama; there is no evident appeal to the people against the elites.
The Wall Street Journal.sesgo: The selection pays particular attention to influential figures, major institutions, legal affairs and education. The New York headline highlights the ideological and economic contrast between its protagonists.

Los Angeles Times.resumen:
- Los Angeles will erect a fence around MacArthur Park amid problems with drugs, violence and homelessness.
- The University of California agrees to provide students and staff with access to ChatGPT, despite faculty concerns.
- Controller Mejia accuses the Los Angeles City Council of trying to reduce Mayor Raman's power.
- Prosecutors will not charge the officer who killed Yong Yang; another trial ends with a conviction for starting a deadly fire in Palisades.
- The front page also covers technology, rescued animals, a storm, centenarians and a commentary on visas for Arab award recipients.
Los Angeles Times.motivo_populismo: The tone is predominantly factual, although expressions such as “desperate,” “sabotage” and “is the honeymoon over?” dramatize some issues.
Los Angeles Times.sesgo: The selection prioritizes local Los Angeles issues and pays attention to social problems, institutional decisions and potential conflicts. It also includes an explicit commentary questioning a claim by RFK Jr. and the difficulties of obtaining a visa.

New York Post.resumen:
- A bedbug infestation at New York City's 911 call center forces the reassignment of police officers.
- Hotel guests sue the co-founder of Angel’s Envy over alleged hidden-camera recordings.
- The front page highlights sports stories about the Giants, Jets and Mets, and the hospitalization of a Titans player.
- Several stories cover the cost of raising a family, Thanksgiving traffic, a burger chain and a drink criticized by Bryan Johnson.
- There is also a Kalshi promotion and coverage of storm-related flooding on a Southern California beach.
New York Post.motivo_populismo: Sensationalist or alarmist expressions such as “brutal,” “desperate” and “How is this legal?” abound, although there is no evident appeal to the people against the elites.
New York Post.sesgo: The selection favors local news, sports, consumer topics and eye-catching incidents, with a focus on entertainment and practical information. There is no clear political bias.

opiniones.comunista:
I see an old contradiction in new clothes on the front pages: artificial intelligence promises to transform the economy while Wall Street celebrates its entry into the stock market and worries about its costs. But who decides how that technology is used, and who will reap its benefits? The University of California's agreement with OpenAI, which faculty members are urging caution over, makes that question urgent.

At the same time, changing funding rules threatens public transportation projects, and a court decision keeps workplace accommodations for pregnant workers on hold in Texas. I stand for the opposite: strong public services, effective labor rights and collective ownership of essential infrastructure. Technology must be under democratic control and serve the working majority, not be subordinated to the profitability of big capital.
opiniones.anarquista:
I see the same impulse in the news: concentrating power and calling it a solution. In Los Angeles, putting a fence around MacArthur Park will not in itself solve homelessness, drugs or violence. I would rather see those who live and work in the neighborhood decide how to organize care, shared space and mutual aid, with resources under community control.

I am also concerned that the University of California is adopting artificial intelligence on a large scale while some faculty members are urging caution. I do not reject technology: I reject decisions affecting learning being made from above, without effective control by those who teach and study. Neither the state nor political parties nor corporations should manage our lives on our behalf. Freedom requires individual autonomy, voluntary cooperation and communities capable of governing themselves without hierarchies.
opiniones.liberal:
I see in today's news a lesson about the limits of power and the virtues of freedom. The training failures identified in the accelerated hiring of immigration officers are a reminder that giving the state more resources and powers does not guarantee competence. Even when exercising its legitimate function of controlling borders, the government must respect individual rights and be accountable for its decisions.

I also welcome the fact that more universities are offering three-year degree programs: competition and the freedom to try different models can ease costs for families without waiting for another bureaucratic solution. And in the face of digital vulnerabilities, companies must take responsibility for protecting their customers. I prefer low taxes, a limited state and responsible citizens and businesses to the illusion that every problem requires a new expansion of government power.
opiniones.extrema_derecha:
Sovereignty is not about promising a tough stance in front of the cameras, but about truly controlling who enters the country and enforcing the law with well-trained officers. The preliminary report on training deficiencies at ICE should concern anyone who supports a secure border: hiring quickly is no substitute for training or accountability. I welcome the fact that the Texas governor-elect and the president are discussing border security; I hope their words translate into firm decisions.

I also want streets and public spaces reclaimed for families. The fence around MacArthur Park may be a useful measure, but it is no substitute for sustained law enforcement. Meanwhile, tech elites promise us wonders from artificial intelligence despite vulnerabilities accumulated over decades. I prefer a country that protects its borders, educates its children and cares for its institutions to one fascinated by every novelty.
opiniones.centro:
I worry that the drive to act quickly will end up weakening the state we need. The draft report on training deficiencies at ICE should prompt a review of the hiring and deployment of officers: an effective immigration policy requires border control, but also respect for due process. Likewise, a health panel that is paralyzed and exposed to potential conflicts of interest serves no one. Its recommendations must be grounded in evidence and independent expertise.

I also believe artificial intelligence can drive prosperity, although digital vulnerabilities and market turbulence remind us that innovation alone is not enough: investment in security and clear rules are needed. I prefer gradual reforms that protect people without stifling private enterprise. The conversation between Trump and the Democratic governor-elect of Texas offers, at least, an opportunity to seek agreement on border security.
